title: The Mesa and the Ice Water: Feynman, the Diagrams, and the Country He Never Reached
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Far Rockaway, the Boy and the Radios

stops.name: New York City, the birth of a physicist his father ordered in advance
stops.date_confidence: Date attested: 11 May 1918 (Wikipedia, 'Richard Feynman'). Place contested and left standing: Wikipedia gives Queens, Britannica and Gleick's Genius give Manhattan. Pinned at a Queens centroid. The research pool's original pin at Far Rockaway is wrong on a third count; the family did not move there until 1927.
stops.campa: Lucille Phillips and Melville Arthur Feynman have a son in New York City on the eleventh of May and name him Richard Phillips. Melville sells uniforms for a living and has wanted a physicist in the family since before the boy existed. He sets Richard on his knee with bathroom tiles, teaches him to lay out patterns, then teaches him to notice that the patterns hold. A second son, Henry Phillips, arrives in 1923 and dies four weeks later. The household observes no religion. Melville drills the boy on the difference between knowing a bird's name and knowing anything about the bird.
sources: James Gleick, Genius: The Life and Science of Richard Feynman (1992)
suggested_refs: The Queens birth record of Richard Phillips Feynman, 11 May 1918, against Britannica's Manhattan

stops.name: New York, the paper weaving and the mother trained to teach it
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to date and place. The kindergarten weaving is Feynman's own account, given to the fifteenth annual meeting of the National Science Teachers Association in New York in 1966 and printed as 'What Is Science?' in The Physics Teacher 7:6 (1969), 313-320; the address was listed as unreached in the first pass of this report and was fetched directly at feynman.com in the Froebel pass of 2026-08-11. He fixes neither the year nor the school, so September 1923, the autumn after his fifth birthday, is an explicit placeholder. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the birth stop above; the family's address before the 1927 move to Far Rockaway is not fixed here. That Lucille Phillips attended the Ethical Culture School is attested (Dictionary of Scientific Biography, 'Feynman, Richard', via encyclopedia.com). That she trained there as a kindergarten teacher is carried at one remove from Gleick's Genius; the text of Genius was not reachable in this pass and the claim is not upgraded.
stops.campa: Lucille Phillips has been schooled at Felix Adler's Ethical Culture School, the institution grown up over the free kindergarten he opened for tenement children in 1878, and is said to have trained there as a kindergartner before her marriage. Her son now goes to kindergarten in his turn and is set to weaving coloured paper strips through vertical strips, which is Friedrich Froebel's occupation carried whole across the Atlantic. He works the pattern out before his hands reach it. The teacher writes home to say the child is unusual. He remembers it forty years later as the first proof that his father's tiles had taken.
stops.quote: We used to weave colored paper through vertical strips and make patterns.
stops.quote_source: 'What Is Science?', address to the fifteenth annual meeting of the National Science Teachers Association, New York, 1966; printed in The Physics Teacher 7:6 (1969), 313-320
sources: Richard Feynman, 'What Is Science?' (1966), The Physics Teacher 7:6 (1969), feynman.com
Dictionary of Scientific Biography, 'Feynman, Richard', via encyclopedia.com
James Gleick, Genius (1992), at one remove
suggested_refs: The Ethical Culture School's training course for kindergartners, and any enrolment record of Lucille Phillips
Froebel's weaving occupation, the paper mats, as taught in American kindergartens before 1930

stops.name: Far Rockaway, the move to the ocean end of Queens
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia, verbatim: 'Four years later, Richard's sister Joan was born and the family moved to Far Rockaway, Queens'). Month and day unknown, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates are a Far Rockaway centroid.
stops.campa: Joan Feynman is born and the family moves out to Far Rockaway, where the Atlantic runs up the sand two streets from the door. Richard is nine. He takes his sister outside at night to look at the aurora and tells her that she is allowed to know things; she grows up to be an astrophysicist. In the back room he assembles a laboratory out of salvaged radios, a rheostat wound by hand, a burglar alarm rigged on his own door. The neighbourhood learns that the Feynman boy will fix a set for nothing if you let him watch it work.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Joan Feynman's own accounts of the aurora and her brother's permission to know things

stops.name: Far Rockaway High School, the algebra team
stops.date_confidence: Span 1931-1935 attested (Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, 1985). The September start is an academic convention and not a documented date. No school record was consulted in this research; the particulars rest on the memoir alone.
stops.campa: He enters Far Rockaway High School, where the algebra team solves problems against the clock without writing anything down. Feynman learns there that a hard question is answered by seeing its shape rather than by grinding at it. He teaches himself trigonometry and calculus out of library books and invents a private notation for functions, which annoys him later when he finds the world already has one. The radios in the back room go on paying for themselves. He tells the whole of these years himself, forty years afterward, into a friend's tape recorder.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Far Rockaway High School records for 1931-1935, not consulted here

stops.name: MIT, mathematics abandoned for physics
stops.date_confidence: Span 1935-1939 attested (Gleick, Genius). September start conventional. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the MIT pin in robert_oppenheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He goes up to Cambridge to read mathematics, decides it is too pure, tries electrical engineering, decides it is too applied, and settles on physics in between. He publishes a paper before he graduates. In 1947 Robert Oppenheimer will stand in these same buildings and tell an audience that the physicists have known sin; Feynman crosses this yard twelve years earlier as an undergraduate who has not been told there is anything yet to know. He takes the bachelor's degree in 1939 and is named a Putnam Fellow the same year, having sat the examination cold.
suggested_refs: Feynman's undergraduate paper, published before the 1939 degree

stops.name: Princeton, Wheeler and the sum over all the routes
stops.date_confidence: Span 1939-1942 attested (Gleick; Feynman's Nobel autobiography, nobelprize.org). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Princeton pin shared by von_neumann.journey.json and robert_oppenheimer.journey.json; Palmer Physical Laboratory itself sits a few hundred metres off that point.
stops.campa: John Archibald Wheeler takes him as a student, and the two set about abolishing the electromagnetic field, proposing that charges act on each other directly across time, forward and backward both. Out of the wreck of that attempt Feynman builds the path integral: a particle goes from here to there by every route at once, and the routes add. Albert Einstein is at the Institute a mile away through all these years. Paul Dirac has worked in the old Fine Hall before him. John von Neumann has been one of the Institute's founding six since 1933.
suggested_refs: The Wheeler-Feynman absorber theory papers, and the 1942 dissertation that grew out of their failure

stops.name: Princeton, the doctorate and the emptying building
stops.date_confidence: Year attested (Wikipedia). Month of the degree not fixed in reachable sources; defaulted to June, the Princeton commencement month. Same inherited coordinates as the previous stop.
stops.campa: The thesis is called The Principle of Least Action in Quantum Mechanics, and it holds, in a form almost nobody reads for six years, everything that will later be drawn as diagrams. Wheeler signs it. Feynman is twenty-four. He has already spent 1941 on ballistics research at the Frankford Arsenal in Pennsylvania, and the physics building around him is emptying into projects with no published address. He is offered a place at one of those within weeks, and he does not ask many questions about it.
suggested_refs: The 1942 Princeton dissertation, unpublished for years and then foundational

stops.name: Staten Island, the city office and the marriage everyone opposed
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 29 June 1942 (Wikipedia, verbatim: 'they took the ferry to Staten Island, where they were married in the city office'). Commonly retold as a wedding on the ferry; the ferry was the transport. Coordinates are the St George borough hall area, approximate. The research pool's Manhattan Municipal Building pin was in fact the generic New York City centroid.
stops.campa: Arline Greenbaum has tuberculosis and will not recover from it. Feynman marries her anyway, over the objection of both families, taking the ferry across the harbour to the city office on Staten Island because that is where the thing can be done. He does not kiss her on the mouth; the doctors have forbidden it. Within a year he will be working at an address he is not permitted to name and she will be lying in a sanatorium in New Mexico a hundred miles from him, and the marriage will be conducted almost entirely by letter, through a censor.
sources: Richard Feynman, What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988)
suggested_refs: The Staten Island city office marriage record, 29 June 1942

stops.name: Los Alamos, up onto the mesa in the last week of March
stops.date_confidence: Departure for Los Alamos attested as 28 March 1943 (Wikipedia). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the mesa pin in robert_oppenheimer.journey.json. Correction to the pool: Feynman was recruited by Robert R. Wilson, not by Oppenheimer, who directed the site.
stops.campa: Robert Wilson, working on enriched uranium, comes to Princeton to recruit him, and Feynman goes up onto the mesa in the last week of March. Robert Oppenheimer runs the place. Hans Bethe takes the twenty-four-year-old into the theoretical division and makes him a group leader, on the grounds that he is the only man in the building who argues back at full volume and is generally right. The buildings of the Los Alamos Ranch School are still standing. The town has no address, one telephone line out, and a censor who reads Arline's letters before Feynman does.
suggested_refs: Robert R. Wilson's recruiting trip to Princeton, spring 1943

stops.name: Los Alamos, Bohr sends for the one man who will contradict him
stops.date_confidence: Bohr's arrival at Los Alamos on 30 December 1943 under the name Nicholas Baker is attested in niels_bohr.journey.json. Feynman's private sessions with him are told in his own memoir and are not separately dated; this stop carries Bohr's arrival date, not a dated meeting. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Bohr pin.
stops.campa: Niels Bohr arrives on the mesa travelling as Nicholas Baker, and the laboratory arranges itself around him in attitudes of reverence. Bohr sends his son ahead to find the young man who is not reverent. Feynman is fetched out and told that the great man wants to try an idea on somebody who will say it is no good if it is no good, and the two of them work through it alone for a couple of hours before the rest of the division is admitted. Feynman is twenty-five and has no notion that he has been selected for anything.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Aage Bohr's recollection of finding Feynman for his father at Los Alamos

stops.name: Los Alamos, the combination locks and the notes left inside
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the Los Alamos years generally as Feynman's own account (Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, 1985; Wikipedia, Los Alamos section). No security log confirming an individual opening was reachable, so 1944-01-01 is a placeholder within 1943-1945. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Los Alamos pin in fermi.journey.json and von_neumann.journey.json.
stops.campa: He opens the safes. The cabinets holding the design of the weapon are fitted with combination locks, and Feynman works out that most officers never change the factory setting, that the last digit can be read off the slack in the dial, and that a man choosing his own combination will use a physical constant. He leaves notes inside the drawers so the owners will know he has been there. The security office responds by circulating an order that Feynman is to be kept out of everyone's rooms, which he records as the whole of what the establishment learned.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Los Alamos security office memoranda of 1943-1945, not reachable in this research

stops.name: Oak Ridge, the Y-12 plant and the stacked uranium
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an episode of 1943-1944 on Feynman's own account (Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!); the visits are not individually dated, so the year stands as a placeholder. Coordinates corrected to the Y-12 plant itself, 35 deg 59'18"N 84 deg 15'17"W; the pool's figure was the town of Oak Ridge, 2.7 km NNW. No plant records were consulted.
stops.campa: He is sent east to the enrichment plant in Tennessee, where separated uranium is being stacked in rooms by men who have not been told what it is and therefore cannot be told what it does. Feynman reads the plant's blueprints cold in front of its engineers, puts a finger on a valve and asks what happens when that one sticks. The drawings are redone. He argues to the army that the workers have to be told enough to be afraid of the right things, and the army agrees to tell them.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Y-12 criticality safety procedures revised after the 1943-1944 Los Alamos visits

stops.name: Los Alamos, the punched cards and the height of burst
stops.date_confidence: Fermi's presence in F Division from 1 September 1944 is attested in fermi.journey.json and supplies this date. Feynman's IBM computing group is attested to the same site and period without a fixed start. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the same file. No corpus journey names Feynman; the crossing is historical, not documented inside these files.
stops.campa: Feynman takes over the implosion calculations and turns a room of women with desk calculators into a machine, colour-coded cards moving through stations in parallel, then feeds the same scheme to the IBM punched-card equipment when it arrives in crates with no instructions in them. Enrico Fermi is in F Division from the autumn, working the same problem by intuition at a blackboard. John von Neumann is on the mesa for the lens and for the height of burst. What the three of them compute is how high above a city the thing should be let off.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: The Los Alamos IBM computing group and its human calculators, T Division, 1944-1945

stops.name: Albuquerque, the sanatorium and the clock he had repaired
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Arline Feynman died 16 June 1945 (Wikipedia; Gleick). Coordinates approximate to central Albuquerque rather than to a surveyed sanatorium building. The clock and the shop window come from What Do You Care What Other People Think? and are memoir, not record.
stops.campa: Arline has lain in the Presbyterian Sanatorium at Albuquerque for two years, a hundred miles down off the mesa, and Feynman has borrowed cars and begged rides to reach her most weekends. He borrows one more when the message comes. She dies in the evening with him sitting beside her. He notes the time from the clock in the room, the same clock he had repaired so that she could see it from the bed. Then he drives back up and works. He does not weep for a month, and when he does it is at a shop window in Oak Ridge with a dress in it.
sources: Richard Feynman, What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988)
suggested_refs: The Presbyterian Sanatorium, Albuquerque, and its 1943-1945 patient records

stops.name: Trinity, the only man watching in colour
stops.date_confidence: Attested: 16 July 1945. Feynman watched from Base Camp, roughly ten to twenty miles from ground zero; the pin is ground zero in the Jornada del Muerto, some two hundred miles south of Los Alamos and sixty miles northwest of the town of Alamogordo. The pool's phrase 'Los Alamos's viewing distance' is meaningless and is discarded. That he alone saw it unprotected is his own claim.
stops.campa: Everyone is issued dark glasses. Feynman reasons that at this distance the only thing that can injure an eye is ultraviolet, that a truck windshield stops ultraviolet, and that he would rather see the thing than be shielded from a danger that is not present. He sits in the cab and watches with his own eyes: white, then yellow, then orange, the cloud climbing and blackening at its edges from the soot it is making. He is the only man there who sees the first nuclear explosion in colour. Afterwards people are shaking hands. Arline has been dead a month.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Trinity Base Camp observer positions, 16 July 1945

stops.name: Cornell, the year he cannot think
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Feynman left Los Alamos for Cornell in October 1945 (Wikipedia). Day of arrival not fixed, defaulted to 01. The paralysis and the blast-radius arithmetic are his own retrospective account.
stops.campa: Bethe brings him to Cornell as an assistant professor, and Feynman discovers that he cannot work. He can teach, he can talk, he can read; he cannot think about physics. He is twenty-seven, a widower, and part-author of a weapon that has now been used twice on cities. He sits in restaurants in Ithaca computing how far the blast radius would reach out from a bridge in New York, and finds that the calculation will not switch itself off. Offers arrive from other universities at salaries that embarrass him, which he takes as proof that they have mistaken him for someone who is working.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Feynman's 1945-1947 Cornell correspondence, on the postwar paralysis

stops.name: Ithaca, the letter to a wife dead sixteen months
stops.date_confidence: Letter dated 17 October 1946, published in Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track (2005) and transcribed at news.lettersofnote.com. Feynman's location on the day is inferred from the Cornell appointment and is not documented. Melville Feynman's death on 8 October 1946 is separately attested (Wikipedia).
stops.campa: His father Melville dies of a stroke on the eighth of October, sixteen months after Arline. Nine days later Feynman sits down and writes a letter to his wife, who has been dead a year and a half, tells her that he has met people and does not want to meet them, that she stands in the way of his loving anyone else, and asks her to excuse him for not posting it, because he does not know her new address. He seals it. It is found among his papers after his own death, unopened, forty-two years later.
stops.quote: I love my wife. My wife is dead.
stops.quote_source: Letter to Arline Feynman, 17 October 1946, in Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track: The Letters of Richard P. Feynman, ed. Michelle Feynman (2005)
sources: Perfectly Reasonable Deviations from the Beaten Track (2005)
suggested_refs: The sealed 1946 letter, opened only after Feynman's death in 1988

stops.name: Shelter Island, the conference under police escort
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Shelter Island Conference ran 2-4 June 1947. Coordinates corrected to the Ram's Head Inn on Ram Island; the pool's figure sat 2.8 km SW on the main body of the island. Wikipedia calls Feynman's contribution an informal presentation, which contradicts the pool's claim that he presented a path-integral treatment of renormalization here. The deflationary version is followed.
stops.campa: Two dozen theorists are driven out to the east end of Long Island with a police escort, because the war has made physicists into people worth escorting. Willis Lamb reports a measured shift in the hydrogen spectrum that the theory says cannot exist. Feynman talks informally about his own way of handling the infinities and is not much attended to. Bethe does the first rough calculation of the Lamb shift on the train home. The renewal of quantum electrodynamics begins in this room, with Feynman in it and not yet at its centre.
sources: Silvan S. Schweber, QED and the Men Who Made It (1994)
suggested_refs: The Ram's Head Inn, Ram Island Drive, Shelter Island, June 1947

stops.name: Pocono Manor, the diagrams shown and rejected
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Pocono Conference ran 30 March to 2 April 1948 at the Pocono Manor Inn, with Bohr and Dirac both challenging Feynman (Schweber). Coordinates corrected to the village of Pocono Manor; the pool's figure lay 4.8 km NE.
stops.campa: Julian Schwinger speaks most of a day in a formalism nobody can fault and few can follow. Feynman then stands up and draws pictures: straight lines for electrons, wavy lines for light, vertices where they meet, and rules for turning the pictures into numbers. Niels Bohr comes up to the blackboard to tell him he has forgotten the exclusion principle and cannot be drawing trajectories at all. Paul Dirac asks whether the thing is unitary and will not let go of the question. Feynman sits down having failed. The diagrams are correct and it will take Freeman Dyson to make the room see it.
sources: Silvan S. Schweber, QED and the Men Who Made It (1994)
suggested_refs: Contemporary notes of the Pocono Conference, 30 March to 2 April 1948

stops.name: Oldstone-on-the-Hudson, Dyson makes the room see it
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Oldstone Conference ran 11-14 April 1949 (Schweber). Location corrected: Oldstone-on-the-Hudson stood in Cortlandt Manor near Peekskill, not at Croton-on-Hudson as the pool had it, which lies roughly 10 km south. Coordinates approximate.
stops.campa: A year after the Poconos the same men reassemble above the Hudson, and Freeman Dyson has in the meantime written the paper showing that Schwinger's formalism and Feynman's pictures are one theory in two suits of clothes. The diagrams pass into general use inside eighteen months, and within a decade nobody calculates any other way. Feynman does not particularly enjoy being explained. He does not object either, because the whole argument for the method is that it works, and this room has now watched it work.
sources: Silvan S. Schweber, QED and the Men Who Made It (1994)
suggested_refs: Freeman Dyson, 'The Radiation Theories of Tomonaga, Schwinger, and Feynman' (1949)

stops.name: Rio de Janeiro, the frying pan and the complaint to the ministry
stops.date_confidence: Sabbatical year at the Centro Brasileiro de Pesquisas Fisicas attested for 1951-1952 (Wikipedia), following several weeks in Rio in July 1949. Month and day of arrival not fixed, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates corrected to the CBPF building in Urca; the pool's figure was a mangled Rio centroid 8 km inland. The pool's separate Copacabana beach pin, tagged as unverified leisure, is folded in here rather than pinned.
stops.campa: He takes a year in Rio, lectures in Portuguese learned for the purpose, and joins a samba school as a frigideira player, beating a small metal frying pan through the streets at Carnival among men who have no idea what he does for a living. At the end of the year he tells the Brazilian ministry to its face that the country is teaching physics by memorised definitions and is therefore producing no physicists. He delivers this at the closing address the ministry has arranged, with the teachers it trains sitting in front of him.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Feynman's closing address to Brazilian science teachers, Rio de Janeiro, 1952

stops.name: Caltech, the office he never leaves
stops.date_confidence: Contradiction inside the research pool, left standing: its chronology gives 1952 for the Caltech professorship, its geography lens gives the span as 1950-1988. Month and day unfixed, defaulted to 01-01. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Pasadena pin shared by einstein.journey.json and robert_oppenheimer.journey.json.
stops.campa: He comes down to Pasadena and does not leave it for thirty-six years, turning down every other offer on the grounds that the weather is good and the physics is next door. Albert Einstein wintered on this campus in the early thirties. Robert Oppenheimer came south to these same buildings each spring from Berkeley. Feynman puts his office where students can walk into it without an appointment and keeps a notebook headed Notebook of Things I Don't Know About, which he means to fill up and then empty.
suggested_refs: Feynman's Caltech appointment file and the date of his arrival, 1950 or 1952

stops.name: Boise, the marriage that goes wrong at once
stops.date_confidence: Attested: married Mary Louise Bell in Boise, Idaho, 28 June 1952; separated 20 May 1956; interlocutory decree 19 June 1956; divorce final 5 May 1958 (all Wikipedia). Coordinates are the city of Boise. The divorce complaint's wording is widely reprinted and was not verified against the court filing in this research.
stops.campa: He marries Mary Louise Bell in Boise, and the marriage is wrong from the first months and stays wrong for four years. She wants a husband who dresses for dinner. He does calculus in his head in the car and drums on whatever is within reach of his hands. They separate in May 1956, an interlocutory decree follows in June, and the divorce is not final until May 1958. The complaint filed against him is said to state that he worked at calculus while driving, in bed, and while sitting in the living room, which would be accurate.
suggested_refs: The 1956 California divorce filing of Mary Louise Bell against Richard Feynman, not consulted here

stops.name: Kyoto, the inn instead of the hotel
stops.date_confidence: Correction to the pool, which dates this September 1955. Feynman's first visit to Japan was for the International Conference of Theoretical Physics held at Kyoto and Tokyo, 14-24 September 1953, organised by the Science Council of Japan under IUPAP auspices, proceedings published 1954. The two-year discrepancy is recorded and the earlier date taken. Kyoto coordinates are exact.
stops.campa: He goes to Japan for the international conference on theoretical physics and refuses the hotel the organisers have booked, staying at a Japanese inn instead, sitting on the floor, learning enough of the language to be rude in it. He comes home saying it is the only country besides his own he could imagine living in. Shin'ichiro Tomonaga is in the room. Tomonaga solved the same problem Feynman solved, in wartime isolation, in a country that was being burned. Twelve years from now the two of them will divide a prize between them and a third man.
sources: Feynman correspondence cited in Gleick, Genius (1992)
Proceedings of the International Conference of Theoretical Physics, Kyoto and Tokyo (1954)
suggested_refs: The 1953 IUPAP conference proceedings, Kyoto and Tokyo, listing the foreign delegates

stops.name: Las Vegas, the only arithmetic on the floor
stops.date_confidence: Attested to the 1950s generally on Feynman's own account (Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!); no individual trip is dated in reachable sources, so 1955-01-01 is an explicit placeholder within the decade. Coordinates are the city.
stops.campa: He drives out to Nevada repeatedly through the decade, establishes that every game on the floor is priced against the player, declines on that basis to play any of them, and spends his time in the lounges instead with the showgirls and the professional gamblers. The professionals interest him because they are the only people in the building doing arithmetic. One of them explains that the whole trade consists of betting only where the odds have been set wrong, and then waiting for the wrong odds to come round again.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Feynman's Las Vegas acquaintance Nick the Greek, as described in the 1985 memoir

stops.name: Geneva, the beach at the Atoms for Peace conference
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the September 1958 Atoms for Peace Conference, where Feynman met Gweneth Howarth on the beach at Lake Geneva (Wikipedia, verbatim). Exact day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Coordinates are the city of Geneva. The pool's separate CERN pin is tagged as unverified in the pool itself and is not used.
stops.campa: The government has had doubts about his clearance and sends him to Switzerland regardless. On the beach at Lake Geneva he meets Gweneth Howarth, a young Englishwoman out of Yorkshire who has left home to see the world and is paying for it by working as a domestic wherever she lands. Feynman offers to employ her as his housekeeper in California, tells her plainly what the arrangement is and what it is not, and sets about the visa. She takes eight months to get there. He is forty and has been on his own since the divorce.
suggested_refs: The Second Atoms for Peace Conference, Geneva, September 1958, delegate lists

stops.name: Altadena, the housekeeper who reports back at breakfast
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Gweneth Howarth arrived in Altadena in June 1959 to work in Feynman's house (Wikipedia). Day not recorded, defaulted to 01. Correction to the pool, which claimed they met in Altadena where she was an au pair; they met at Lake Geneva in 1958 and this is where the courtship continued.
stops.campa: She arrives in June and takes the housekeeper's post at the house north of Pasadena. Feynman goes on seeing other women and reports on them to her over breakfast; she takes up with other men and reports back in kind. The arrangement runs a year and then stops being an arrangement. His friends expect the usual scandal of a professor and his domestic help. What they find is two people who tell each other everything and let the neighbourhood make of it what it likes.
suggested_refs: Gweneth Howarth's 1959 immigration and employment papers

stops.name: Pasadena, the Huntington Hotel and the last marriage
stops.date_confidence: Attested: married Gweneth Howarth at the Huntington Hotel, Pasadena, 24 September 1960 (Wikipedia). Carl born 1962, Michelle adopted 1968 (Wikipedia). Coordinates are the hotel. The household itself was in Altadena, not Pasadena, from 1960 until his death; the pool's Alameda Street pin near Caltech is wrong on the town.
stops.campa: They marry at the Huntington on the twenty-fourth of September. Carl is born in 1962, Michelle is adopted in 1968, and the family settles in Altadena in a house full of drums, blackboards, and Gweneth's flat refusal to let a professor be excused from carrying out the rubbish. The marriage lasts twenty-eight years and ends with his death. Of the three wives, the first he could not keep and the second he could not talk to. This one travels with him to Stockholm, to the Soviet embassies, and to the hospital.
sources: Jagdish Mehra, The Beat of a Different Drum (1994)
suggested_refs: The Huntington Hotel, Pasadena, wedding register for 24 September 1960

stops.name: Caltech, two years of chalk and no notes
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Feynman delivered the introductory course from 1961, published as The Feynman Lectures on Physics; the pool's afterlife lens gives the course span as 1961-1964 and its chronology gives 1961. September start is the academic convention. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus Pasadena pin.
stops.campa: Caltech asks him to rebuild the two-year introductory course, and he builds it from nothing, standing in front of first-year students twice a week for two years with a piece of chalk. The lectures are recorded and transcribed as they are given. As a course for beginners it is generally judged to have failed: the beginners fall away and graduate students and faculty fill the seats behind them. As a book it never goes out of print, it is translated into Spanish among many other languages, and physicists keep it within arm's reach for the rest of the century.
suggested_refs: The original Caltech recordings of the 1961-1963 introductory course

stops.name: Stockholm, the prize divided three ways
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the 1965 Nobel Prize in Physics, shared with Julian Schwinger and Shin'ichiro Tomonaga, presented 10 December 1965 (Nobel Foundation). Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Stockholm Concert Hall pin shared by fermi.journey.json, dirac.journey.json, niels_bohr.journey.json and heisenberg.journey.json. The predawn telephone call is Feynman's own repeated telling; no dialogue is reproduced here.
stops.campa: A reporter telephones before dawn to tell him he has won, and Feynman asks why it could not have waited until morning. He considers refusing the thing outright, on the ground that the honour of the work is the pleasure of finding it out and everything afterwards is bookkeeping, then accepts, because refusing would make more noise than accepting. Niels Bohr took the prize in this hall in 1922, Paul Dirac and Werner Heisenberg in 1933, Enrico Fermi in 1938. Feynman wears the tails and bows to the king. Schwinger and Tomonaga, who reached the same answer by other roads, stand beside him.
suggested_refs: The 1965 Nobel Lecture, 'The Development of the Space-Time View of Quantum Electrodynamics'

stops.name: Caltech, the charge that the record does not answer
stops.date_confidence: Attested only as a bare fact: Feynman and other faculty faced controversy in 1968 over allegations of sexism toward women at Caltech (Wikipedia). No reachable source gives complainants, particulars, process, or finding, and no month is recorded; defaulted to 01-01. The gap is large and is stated as a gap. The topless bar is a separate matter from his own memoir and is not offered as evidence either way.
stops.campa: Allegations of sexism toward women at Caltech are made against Feynman and against other members of the faculty. The reachable record gives the accusation and nothing else: no names, no hearing, no finding, no year's end to it. It sits in the same years as the lectures and the drumming and the bar out on the highway where he does arithmetic on paper placemats and which he defends in court when the county moves to shut it. The charge stands recorded because it was made, with nothing available to settle it.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Caltech records of the 1968 complaints, not reachable in this research

segments.name: The Van, the Knife, and Tuva

stops.name: Big Sur, the baths and the question about the pituitary
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Feynman's visits to Esalen are attested in his own writing but are not dated in reachable sources; 1970-01-01 is an explicit placeholder for the 1960s and 1970s. Coordinates corrected to the institute on Highway One at 36 deg 07'37"N 121 deg 38'30"W; the pool's figure fell about 13 km offshore in the Pacific.
stops.campa: He drives up the coast to the hot springs at Big Sur, where the human potential movement holds its workshops on the cliff above the water, and sits in the baths listening to a woman explain that she is working a meridian in a foot and that the foot connects to the pituitary. Feynman asks her where the pituitary is. She is not sure. He tells her it is in the brain, and she answers that everything is connected anyway. He keeps going back. He likes the baths and he will talk to anybody, and he goes on asking where the pituitary is.
sources: Richard Feynman, Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! (1985)
suggested_refs: Esalen Institute workshop records for the years Feynman visited, undated in reachable sources

stops.name: Caltech, cargo cult science at commencement
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the 1974 Caltech commencement address 'Cargo Cult Science', published in Engineering and Science and held by the Caltech Archives, fetched directly at calteches.library.caltech.edu. The exact ceremony date was not confirmed; June is the Caltech commencement month. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the corpus Pasadena pin.
stops.campa: He tells the graduating class about islanders who cut runways out of the bush and light fires along them and wait for cargo planes that do not come, because the form was copied faithfully and the thing that made the form work was never understood. Then he turns it on their own profession: the experiments that never report the runs that failed, the psychology that will not repeat an old result, the advertising that is technically true. He gives them one rule and tells them the rest follows from it.
stops.quote: The first principle is that you must not fool yourself—and you are the easiest person to fool.
stops.quote_source: 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech commencement address (1974), published in Engineering and Science; text held by Caltech Archives
sources: 'Cargo Cult Science', Caltech commencement address (1974), Caltech Archives
suggested_refs: The Engineering and Science printing of 'Cargo Cult Science', 1974

stops.name: Long Beach, the van with the diagrams on it
stops.date_confidence: Attested for 1975, with the place given as Long Beach, California (Wikipedia). Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01; coordinates are the city rather than a documented shop. Seamus Blackley's purchase and preservation of the van in 2012 is separately attested.
stops.campa: He has a Dodge Tradesman Maxivan painted over with his own diagrams, wavy photon lines and electron arrows running the whole length of the bodywork, and drives it around Pasadena with the plate QANTUM. Asked at a traffic light why his van is covered in squiggles, he answers that they are Feynman diagrams. Asked who Feynman is, he says that he is Feynman. The van outlives him. Seamus Blackley buys the van in 2012, restores it, and has kept it in public view since.
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of things named after Richard Feynman'
suggested_refs: The Feynvan, restored and exhibited since 2012

stops.name: UCLA Medical Center, the tumour that crushed a kidney
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the research pool's tag of reconstruction is corrected here to attested: Wikipedia states directly that in 1978 Feynman was diagnosed with liposarcoma and that surgeons removed a 'very large' tumour that had crushed one kidney and his spleen. Month not recorded, defaulted to 01-01. 'The size of a football' is Gleick's phrasing, not Wikipedia's, and the organs were crushed rather than removed alongside.
stops.campa: The pain in his abdomen turns out to be a liposarcoma, a cancer rare enough that his surgeon will see few others in a career. They take out a mass that has crushed one kidney and his spleen. He asks for the numbers, is given survival statistics that are not encouraging, and works out for himself that the sample is small enough that the statistics do not mean very much either. Then he goes back to teaching. The disease returns twice in the ten years left to him, and each time he treats it as an interruption of the work rather than as the work.
suggested_refs: UCLA Medical Center surgical records, 1978, not consulted here

stops.name: Moscow, ten years of letters into a ministry
stops.date_confidence: Attested that Feynman and Ralph Leighton pursued years of bureaucratic correspondence for passage to Tuva (Leighton, Tuva or Bust!, 1991). The campaign has no single date; 1980-01-01 is an explicit placeholder within the decade. The pin stands for the route the requests travelled, not for a visit; Feynman never went to the Soviet Union on this business.
stops.campa: It begins as a puzzle: a country whose capital is spelled Kyzyl, with no honest vowel in it, which issues diamond-shaped postage stamps and which nobody Feynman knows can point to on a map. He and Ralph Leighton resolve to go there and spend ten years being handled by Soviet ministries, learning Tuvan out of a grammar, writing to academicians, posting letters into a system built to absorb them without trace. The refusals are never quite refusals. Neither man ever boards a plane, and the file goes on thickening until Feynman is dying.
suggested_refs: The Feynman-Leighton Tuva correspondence files, 1977-1988

stops.name: Altadena, the tape recorder running beside the drums
stops.date_confidence: Both Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman! and QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter were published in 1985 (Wikipedia); QED derives from the Alix G. Mautner Memorial Lectures. The taping sessions with Ralph Leighton ran over several years and are not individually dated, so the date is the publication year and the pin is the Altadena household.
stops.campa: For years Feynman and Ralph Leighton have drummed together once a week, and for years Leighton has kept a tape running while Feynman talks. The transcripts become Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!, published in 1985, which sells in numbers no physics paper approaches and fixes his public shape for good: the safecracker, the bongo player, the man who declines to be impressed. The same year he publishes QED, four lectures explaining the theory he was given the prize for to readers with no mathematics, using nothing but little arrows that add up.
sources: Richard Feynman, QED: The Strange Theory of Light and Matter (1985)
suggested_refs: The Leighton tapes behind Surely You're Joking, Mr. Feynman!

stops.name: Cape Canaveral, seventy-three seconds
stops.date_confidence: Attested: Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch on 28 January 1986, killing all seven crew; the cause was traced to failure of an O-ring seal (Rogers Commission Report). Coordinates are Launch Complex 39B at the Kennedy Space Center.
stops.campa: It is cold on the Florida coast that morning, cold enough to leave ice on the tower. Challenger lifts and comes apart seventy-three seconds later, and seven people are killed in front of a television audience that includes most of the schoolrooms in the country, because a schoolteacher is aboard. The joints of the solid rocket boosters are sealed by rubber O-rings. The overnight temperature has been below freezing. The engineers who said so the night before were asked to take off their engineering hat and put on their management hat, and were overruled.
suggested_refs: The Thiokol teleconference of 27 January 1986, transcribed in the Rogers Commission Report

stops.name: Washington, the commissioner who telephones the engineers himself
stops.date_confidence: Feynman's appointment to the Rogers Commission in 1986 is attested (Wikipedia); the exact date is not fixed in reachable sources and 3 February is taken from the commission's formation, hedged. Coordinates inherited byte-identical from the Washington pin in niels_bohr.journey.json.
stops.campa: Gweneth tells him to take it, on the grounds that everybody else appointed will do the polite thing and he will not. He is sixty-seven years old and has cancer. He goes to Washington, declines the prepared schedule of briefings, and starts telephoning engineers at the contractors directly, asking them what they had been worried about and writing the answers in a notebook. Niels Bohr passed through this city under an alias in December 1943 on his way to the mesa. John von Neumann died in a hospital here in 1957.
stops.quote: Without detailed understanding, confidence can not be attained.
stops.quote_source: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 2, Appendix F, 'Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle' (1986)
suggested_refs: Feynman's own account of the commission in What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988)

stops.name: Washington, the glass of ice water
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the televised hearing of 11 February 1986. Location corrected to the Dean Acheson Auditorium at the Department of State, 2201 C St NW; no source was found placing the hearings at the Department of Transportation, and the pool's National Academy of Sciences label names the wrong institution though its coordinates fall only 250 m away. The clamp was bought near his Washington hotel the night before; the pool's Pasadena kitchen rehearsal is unsupported.
stops.campa: He buys a small C-clamp and a pair of pliers at a hardware store near his hotel and tries the thing out in his room the night before. At the hearing he asks for a glass of ice water, takes a sample of the O-ring rubber out of the model lying on the table, squeezes it flat in the clamp and drops it in the glass. When he lifts it out it does not spring back. He says so into the microphone with the cameras running: for more than a few seconds, at this temperature, the material has no resilience. The commission's finding is made in public before the commission has written it.
stops.quote: Erosion was a clue that something was wrong. Erosion was not something from which safety can be inferred.
stops.quote_source: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 2, Appendix F, 'Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle' (1986)
sources: Broadcast footage of the hearing of 11 February 1986
Richard Feynman, What Do You Care What Other People Think? (1988)
suggested_refs: The Dean Acheson Auditorium, Harry S Truman Building, and the televised session of 11 February 1986

stops.name: Washington, Appendix F at the back of the report
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the Rogers Commission report was delivered in June 1986 with Feynman's 'Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle' appended as Appendix F; text fetched directly from nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v2appf.htm. Exact day defaulted to 01. That he threatened to remove his name unless the appendix was included is widely reported and no primary document of the threat was reached.
stops.campa: The commission's draft says what commissions say. Feynman writes his own account instead: that management put the odds of losing a shuttle at one in a hundred thousand while its own engineers put them at one in a hundred, that erosion found on the seals was read as evidence of safety rather than of danger, that a known weakness accepted often enough stops being visible to the people accepting it. Rogers wants it out of the report. Feynman says his name can come out with it. The appendix goes in at the back, unedited.
stops.quote: For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public relations, for nature cannot be fooled.
stops.quote_source: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 2, Appendix F, 'Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle' (1986), closing line
sources: Rogers Commission Report, Vol. 2, Appendix F (1986), nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v2appf.htm
suggested_refs: Appendix F in full, as printed at the back of the Rogers Commission Report

stops.name: UCLA Medical Center, dialysis refused
stops.date_confidence: Attested: died 15 February 1988 at UCLA Medical Center, aged 69. The immediate cause was a ruptured duodenal ulcer and kidney failure with dialysis refused, and a second cancer, Waldenstrom's macroglobulinemia, was also present. Coordinates corrected from the pool's figure, which was the downtown Los Angeles centroid. The reported last words are not traced to a primary document and are given as reported speech, not as a verified quotation.
stops.campa: The liposarcoma comes back a third time and there is a second cancer beside it. A duodenal ulcer ruptures. His remaining kidney fails and dialysis is offered, and he declines it, having decided that he would rather not spend what is left of him being kept going. He is unconscious for a week. He dies on the fifteenth of February at sixty-nine, with Gweneth and his sister Joan in the room. The line the world remembers him saying near the end is that he would hate to die twice, because it is so boring.
suggested_refs: The UCLA Medical Center death record, 15 February 1988

stops.name: Kyzyl, the permission that arrives too late
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and a destination never reached. The Tuvan invitation is generally said to have arrived within days or a few weeks of Feynman's death and the accounts disagree; the date carried here is his death date, not an arrival, because no arrival occurred. Coordinates are Kyzyl.
stops.campa: Two days after he dies, or a few weeks after, depending on which account is followed, the letter comes through from Moscow: an exchange with the Tuvan Autonomous Republic is permitted, and Richard Feynman may travel to Kyzyl. Ten years of correspondence have worked, and the man they worked for is not there to be told about it. Gweneth and Ralph Leighton make the journey later without him. In the middle of Kyzyl stands a monument declaring the spot the geographic centre of Asia. The claim has never been settled.
suggested_refs: The 1988 Soviet exchange authorisation for Tuva, arriving after Feynman's death

stops.name: Altadena, Mountain View Cemetery and the flat stone
stops.date_confidence: Burial at Mountain View Cemetery and Mausoleum, Altadena, is attested (Wikipedia), but no reachable source fixes the day; 18 February is an inference from the date of death and nothing more. Coordinates corrected to the cemetery at 2400 N Fair Oaks Ave; the pool's figure was the Altadena town centroid, about 1.1 km east.
stops.campa: He is buried in Altadena, a mile and a half from the house, under a small flat stone carrying his name and his dates and nothing else. There is no epitaph. Asteroid 7495 is named for him, and so is a prize in nanotechnology, for a talk he gave in 1959 about writing the encyclopaedia on the head of a pin. In 1999 a poll of a hundred and thirty physicists conducted by Physics World puts him seventh of all time. The van with the diagrams painted down its side is still on the road.
sources: Wikipedia, 'List of things named after Richard Feynman'
suggested_refs: The Feynman grave at Mountain View Cemetery, Altadena, and the 1959 talk 'There's Plenty of Room at the Bottom'
